summary: Hampton Roads entrance light at the edge of Fort Monroe: stone tower of 1802-1803, keepers that include women and a former slave, automated 1972 or 1973, grounds open, tower closed.

structures.note: Height disputed: 54 ft (LighthouseFriends); 40 ft from base to lantern centre, 48 ft above the water (USLHS); the record's 17.5 m is not confirmed by either. No height_m is given until a primary record settles it.
Rebuilt: LighthouseFriends gives 1891; the Board's report for the year ended 30 June 1892 records the rebuilding during April-June 1892; USLHS gives 1900. The disagreement is stated in the story.

access.note: Grounds open; dwelling and tower closed. Reached through Fort Monroe National Monument via McNair Drive.

facts.agency: US Coast Guard (owner), within Fort Monroe National Monument (National Park Service)

events.note: USLHS dates the station and tower to 1802; LighthouseFriends says Burroughs completed most of the tower in 1803
Eli Vickery appointed first keeper on 11 February 1804
Fourth-order Henry-Lepaute Fresnel lens replaced the lamps and reflectors (LighthouseFriends 1854; USLHS gives 1855)
Fog bell mounted on a wooden tower beside the lighthouse, 20 July 1855
Old keeper's dwelling rebuilt: the Board's report for FY1892 records repairs by a working party in April, May and June 1892; LighthouseFriends dates the new house to 1891 (see resolved conflicts)
Wooden fog-bell tower replaced with an iron structure; iron oil house erected
Tower lantern and gallery painted in July 1900 (Board report for the year ended 30 June 1901); old brick replaced
Electric striker replaces the mechanical fog-bell striker
Illuminant changed from oil to electric incandescent
Photoelectric control of the fog bell, beam from Fort Wool
Automated per USLHS; LighthouseFriends says 1973 (see resolved conflicts)
Fort Monroe closed as an Army post in September 2011; designated a national monument and transferred to the National Park Service in November 2011
Grading of the ground around the dwelling (about 50 cart loads of earth, June 1893) and about 300 running feet of galvanized iron pipe laid to connect the station with Fort Monroe's water supply
Colour of light changed 10 March 1899 (Board list of changes); LighthouseFriends dates the change to red about 1900
Hailstorm on the afternoon of 11 May: two windowpanes broken; hailstones as large as hens' eggs reported by the keeper

corrections.why: The record name is the keeper's dwelling. The light is known as Old Point Comfort Light (LighthouseFriends; USLHS place record).
The USLHS record gives the location county as Hampton. Hampton is an independent city in Virginia, not a county.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The record gives 1802 and 1804. The USLHS record dates the station and tower to 1802. LighthouseFriends says the tower was mostly complete in 1803 and the first keeper was appointed on 11 February 1804. No source read gives a first-lighting date, so the record's first_lit should be checked against a Coast Guard List of Lights or a Board report.

The record's dwelling date of 1900 (USLHS) conflicts with LighthouseFriends (1891) and with the Board's report for the year ended 30 June 1892, which records a working party making repairs in April, May and June 1892 and the dwelling rebuilt with new outbuildings. The Board's FY1892 entry is the primary record for the rebuilding and is preferred to the 1891 date; the story gives 1891 and 1892 and the 1900 USLHS date.
USLHS gives 1972 and LighthouseFriends says the dwelling housed Coast Guard families until automation in 1973. The story gives both years and the record's 1972 stands unresolved.
LighthouseFriends dates the fourth-order lens to 1854; USLHS gives 1855.

LighthouseFriends says the light changed from fixed white to fixed red about 1900, showed a white sector in 1905 and then went back to red. The Board's list of changes records a colour change on 10 March 1899, which fits neither date exactly. The story gives both and does not choose.

notes_for_editor: Unresolved: the tower height (LighthouseFriends 54 ft; USLHS 40 ft to the lantern centre and 48 ft above water; the record's 17.5 m). No height_m is published. The record's characteristic 'Fl(2) W 12s' is not supported by any source read here: LighthouseFriends describes a fixed red light with a white sector of 133 degrees in the automated signal, changed several times since about 1900; the Board's 1899 list records a colour change on 10 March 1899. A Coast Guard List of Lights entry is needed. The NRHP nomination (NRIS 73002212) is not digitised (npgallery placeholder), so the 1973 NRHP listing and the historic district status are not sourced here. The record's name Keeper's House is the dwelling; the lighthouse is Old Point Comfort Light. Local unit should read Hampton (independent city). The Board's FY1893 entry is cited by scan page 119 (the grading and water pipe, 'In June'); the FY1899 colour change is cited to the volume only, because the archive's page index is missing for that volume. The Board volumes in the corpus begin in 1891, so the 1802-1890 chapters rest on LighthouseFriends and the USLHS record. The 1886 earthquake, the William Davis and John Jones personal stories and the 1954 bulb episode come from LighthouseFriends alone. The roster matched by position (0.24 km). Coast Guard personnel after 1960 appear only as roster lines with no personal detail. The 1931 hailstorm is from the Bulletin's own station item; no keeper's log was read. A Chronicling America search for 1886 returned no relevant page. Wikipedia was used for leads only and is not cited. Fact-check 2026-10-22: the earlier draft dated the rebuilt dwelling to 1891 as if the Board's report confirmed it; the Board's FY1892 entry (scan p. 118) gives April-June 1892, so the story now states both dates. The 1886 earthquake account is LighthouseFriends' paraphrase of Jones (not a quotation), and the story now attributes it that way. Post-1960 Coast Guard names appear in the roster only; the story no longer names the last keeper in prose.
